newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - July 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - July 14.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- EC DEMANDS CONCESSIONS ON THE TABLE FROM BOEING

The European Commission has warned US aerospace giant Boeing that it needs to lodge its concessions with them by Monday night if the commission is to make a decision on the company's proposed merger with McDonnell-Douglas by July 23, as requested by Boeing. The Commission is seeking evidence of real structural changes to the proposed merger in order to satisfy competition rules.
-- ARNAULT PLANS HIS NEXT MOVE

Bernard Arnault, chairman of French luxury goods firm LVMH, will this week present written proposals to Guinness and Grand Metropolitan as to how to proceed with a three-way alliance between the groups. It is understood that Arnault, who is opposed to the merger between Guinness and GrandMet, has more detailed proposals involving LVMH's Moet and Hennessey brands than originally presented to the other two groups.
-- SKY MAY TAKE MAJOR STAKE IN FORMULA ONE

Satellite broadcaster BSkyB is reported to be considering an investment in Formula One Holdings, the Grand Prix group that Bernie Ecclestone hopes to launch on the stock market this autumn. It is understood that the two parties have discussed a deal in which BSkyB would take a stake in Formula One and gain the right to show Grand Prix racing on pay-per-view over its digital network in the UK next year.
THE TIMES
-- SUPERMARKETS MUST SHARE PETROL BURDEN, SAY OIL FIRMS

Integrated oil groups are expected later this month to tell the Office of Fair Trading Inquiry into the petrol market that current legislation gives an unfair advantage to independent petrol retailers. The groups are likely to call for supermarket chains to be forced to store much larger quantities of petrol as their contribution to ensuring continuity of supply in the event of war.
-- DISCOVERY TO LAUNCH THEMED RETAILERS

US documentary maker Discovery is to launch a chain of nature and science-themed retailers in the UK and continental Europe. The group, which recently formed a $500 million (295 million stg) joint programming venture with the BBC, is making the move after acquiring the Nature Company chain of stores in the US last year, which it plans to recast as Discovery outlets selling products related to the channel.
-- HOPES FOR 'PLASTIC EURO' FADE

The European Commission has scrapped plans to print the new euro notes on plastic. The moves follows warnings from banknote printers that the ink can come off easily, as happened in Australia when plastic notes were introduced there. According to security printers De La Rue, plastic notes last an average of 32 months compared to 18 for paper, but paper notes are half as expensive to produce.
THE GUARDIAN
-- NATWEST PRESSED TO ALTER STRATEGY

Leading shareholders in National Westminster Bank are urging the group to restructure its entire strategy in an attempt to move itself clear of takeover speculation. Among the demands are calls by some institutions for NatWest to replace several non-executive directors after questions were asked about their calibre for a top banking group.
-- BA FACES NEW 3-DAY STRIKE THREAT

Trade union leaders of 9,000 British Airways cabin crew have threatened the company with another three-day stoppage unless it ends the suspension of last weeks' strikers. The threat comes as ground crew at the airline are due to meet Monday to decide whether to call their own strikes in protest at the company's plans to sell off its catering operations.
-- BOOKSELLER TURNS OVER LOYALTY LEAF

WH Smith, the troubled retail group that is still desperately searching for a chief executive to replace the departing Bill Cockburn, is expected this week to unveil a 'Clubcard' loyalty scheme. The move, the first major initiative from new managing director of retail Beverley Hodson, is an attempt to bolster the group's core business and ward off rumoured takeover offers.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- RATES 'MUST REACH 10 PERCENT TO LEVEL HOUSE PRICE INFLATION'

A survey published by the Centre for Economics and Business Research has predicted that interest rates will need to climb to 10 percent in order to level off house price inflation. The survey was supported by Dun & Bradstreet, whose own research reveals that more than half Britain's senior managers expected interest rates to rise above 7 per cent by the end of the year.
-- BRITISH LAND ATTACKED OVER INCENTIVE SCHEME

John Ritblat, the chairman of property company British Land, is expected to face criticism at the group's annual meeting Monday over an incentive scheme for directors. Under the proposed scheme -- which Pirc, the corporate governance lobby group, is urging BL shareholders to oppose -- directors would be given free shares as a reward for their long-term performance.
-- LITTLEWOODS FACES WRIT AFTER BRIBERY CASE FAILS

Littlewoods, the privately owned stores and football pools company, is to be sued by one of its UK consultants after it was revealed that he was arrested on the basis of information supplied to police in Singapore by the group. The consultant, Nicholas Leese, was charged in Singapore with taking bribes, but the case was thrown out of court last month.
